fleetMemoryScratch.text: A dispatch's or a prior lane's own close's claim about a write gate's behavior is a hypothesis about CODE, not a fact -- read the literal SQL/branching before designing a 'corrected re-run' on top of it. Here 'the writer is already gated never to regress an earned cell, so a corrected re-run moves only cells still sitting absent-verified' was false as a description of the actual WHERE clause (unaccounted-only); the correction was found by reading the code and confirmed by one live query, before any implementation, not discovered mid-apply.

When a fix must distinguish 'first-time write' from 'a re-visit of a state I already wrote once,' the code needs to read the TARGET cell's own current state, not just its upstream dependency's state (this job already read zoningDistrict's current state, but never maxHeightFt/maxLotCoveragePct/maxFootprintSqFt's own current state, because first-run semantics never needed to know it). A gate that only widens the SQL WHERE clause without this distinction will re-write a correct cell's timestamp on every re-run even when its content doesn't change -- 'touching' it in exactly the sense the ruling forbade.

Generate a checked-in classification/lookup table by RUNNING the canonical instrument's own function (via runpy/subprocess capture of the live object, not a hand port) and asserting its aggregate output matches the instrument's own printed tally before trusting a single row -- zero risk of the two ever silently diverging (this program's own CTRL-1 lesson, applied to a data table instead of two code paths).

A footprint/derived rail's remediation decision should be computed from its blocking input's SAME-PASS in-memory target state, not a separate query keyed only on a generic 'blockedOn' string -- the string alone doesn't encode WHY it's blocked, and a future unrelated blocking reason sharing the same string would otherwise get swept in.
